hero.basedOn: Randomised trial: 176 psychology students in Malaysia (64% women, average age 21) who watched porn at least 3 times a week. 86 were asked to stop for 7 days and 90 kept watching; craving, mood and withdrawal were checked every night. No measurable withdrawal showed up.
hero.caveat: Most of them were not hooked: 85% scored below the problem cut-off, and 45% of the stop group watched anyway. In an extra check, daily users with high problem scores who stopped felt more craving, so this does not show that hooked daily users get no withdrawal.

ref.cite: Fernandez DP, Kuss DJ, Justice LV, Fernandez EF, Griffiths MD (2023). Effects of a 7-day pornography abstinence period on withdrawal-related symptoms in regular pornography users: a randomized controlled study. Archives of Sexual Behavior 52:1819-1840.
ref.quote: A total of 176 undergraduate students (64.2% female) who were regular pornography users (defined as having used pornography ≥ three times a week in the past 4 weeks)

hero.check: Matches the full text: 176 regular users (64.2% female, Malaysia), no significant group effects and no evidence of withdrawal; 84.7% below the PPCS cut-off of 76; 39 of 86 (45.4%) in the stop group used porn; exploratory abstinence effect on craving at high PPU with daily use.

stats.line: About 11% of US men agree, at least somewhat, with the sentence 'I am addicted to pornography'.
stats.mirror: You've quietly called yourself a porn addict.

basis.design: national survey, online panel matched to US census norms (Qualtrics)
basis.who: US adult internet users, men and women
basis.n: 1,016 men (of 2,075 adults surveyed)
basis.measured: Answering 'somewhat agree', 'agree' or 'strongly agree' to the sentence 'I am addicted to pornography'.

stats.caveat: Feeling addicted is not a diagnosis. In this study the feeling tracked religiousness and moral disapproval of porn, as well as how much people watched.

ref.cite: Grubbs JB, Kraus SW, Perry SL (2019). Self-reported addiction to pornography in a nationally representative sample: the roles of use habits, religiousness, and moral incongruence. Journal of Behavioral Addictions 8:88-93.
ref.quote: roughly 11% of men and 3% of women reported some agreement with the statement “I am addicted to pornography.”

stats.line: Of Swiss men in their mid-20s who watch monthly, 43% admit at least one of six addiction signs; 9% admit three or more.
stats.mirror: You've noticed a warning sign or two in how you watch.

basis.design: national cohort study (C-SURF); questionnaire
basis.who: young Swiss men who visit porn sites at least monthly; average age 25
basis.n: 4,190 men who watch at least monthly (of 5,332 surveyed)
basis.measured: Six true/false statements (Internet Sex Screening Test): continued use, using it to change mood, loss of control, preoccupation, withdrawal, consequences.

stats.caveat: This scale has no agreed cut-off, so this is not a count of addicts. One sign can be mild.

ref.cite: Studer J, Marmet S, Wicki M, Gmel G (2019). Cybersex use and problematic cybersex use among young Swiss men: associations with sociodemographic, sexual, and psychological factors. Journal of Behavioral Addictions 8:794-803.
ref.quote: One or more PCU statement endorsed ( N , %) 1,793 42.8 Three or more PCU statements endorsed ( N , %) 374 8.9

stats.line: In a US national sample, 8% of men watched porn daily or more, and another 15% a few times a week.
stats.mirror: You watch porn every day and wonder how rare that is.

basis.design: national survey, online panel matched to US census norms (Qualtrics)
basis.who: US adult internet users, men and women
basis.n: 1,016 men (of 2,075 adults surveyed)
basis.measured: Answer to 'Within the past year, how often have you viewed pornography?': 'once a day or more' (8% of men) and 'a few times a week' (15%).

stats.caveat: Self-report about a private habit, so the real share may be higher. 'Daily' means once a day or more, over the past year.

ref.cite: Grubbs JB, Kraus SW, Perry SL (2019). Self-reported addiction to pornography in a nationally representative sample: the roles of use habits, religiousness, and moral incongruence. Journal of Behavioral Addictions 8:88-93.

stats.line: In one large US online sample, 91.5% of men had watched porn in the past month.
stats.mirror: You think you're one of the few men who watch porn.

basis.design: online survey (not a random national sample)
basis.who: US adults aged 18 to 73 on Amazon Mechanical Turk, men and women
basis.n: 1,392 adults (men and women; the study summary doesn't say how many were men)
basis.measured: Any porn in the past month, in any form: videos, pictures or written.

stats.caveat: Paid online-task workers, not a random sample. A census-matched US survey found 59% of men watched at least monthly in 2019. Counts any use, not problems.

ref.cite: Solano I, Eaton NR, O'Leary KD (2020). Pornography consumption, modality and function in a large internet sample. Journal of Sex Research 57:92-103.
ref.quote: Using all modalities of pornography, 91.5% of men and 60.2% of women herein reported having consumed pornography in the past month.

stats.line: About 4 in 5 Swiss men in their mid-20s visit porn sites at least once a month.
stats.mirror: You visit porn sites every month and assume every guy does.

basis.design: national cohort study (C-SURF); questionnaire
basis.who: young Swiss men first enrolled at the compulsory army fitness check; average age 25
basis.measured: Visiting porn websites at least once a month in the past 12 months.

stats.caveat: Men only, one country. 'Monthly' is a low bar and says nothing about problems; among these users the average was about 10 days a month.

ref.cite: Studer J, Marmet S, Wicki M, Gmel G (2019). Cybersex use and problematic cybersex use among young Swiss men: associations with sociodemographic, sexual, and psychological factors. Journal of Behavioral Addictions 8:794-803.
ref.quote: At least monthly CU was reported by 78.6% of participants.

stats.line: Young people in England first saw porn at 13 on average; 1 in 10 had seen it by age 9.
stats.mirror: You were 13 or younger the first time you saw porn.

basis.design: survey plus focus groups, run for the Children's Commissioner
basis.who: young people aged 16 to 21, boys and girls; the age figures are for those who had seen online porn
basis.n: about 650 who had seen porn (64% of 1,014 surveyed, 477 of them male)
basis.measured: The age they remember first seeing porn.

stats.caveat: Remembered years later. Boys and girls together, but the report found no difference between them. Says when it starts, not who goes on to have a problem.

ref.cite: Children's Commissioner for England (2023). 'A lot of it is actually just abuse': young people and pornography.
ref.quote: The average age at which children first see pornography is 13. By age nine, 10% had seen pornography, 27% had seen it by age 11

stats.line: Young adults with both low mood and anxiety had about 2.7 times the odds of watching porn daily, rather than never, six months later.
stats.mirror: You reach for porn when you feel low and wound up.

basis.design: cohort followed for 6 months (Happiness & Health Study)
basis.who: young adults first enrolled in 9th grade at 10 Los Angeles-area high schools in 2013; men and women
basis.n: 1,399 young adults: 803 with both low mood and anxiety, 596 with neither (of 1,864 followed)
basis.when: March to September 2020, then January to June 2021
basis.measured: Depression and anxiety symptoms at the start; how often they watched porn six months later.

stats.caveat: Odds, not chance. Men and women mixed, measured during the pandemic; low mood alone was not significant. This figure allows for gender, sexual orientation, sexual satisfaction and hard childhoods; without that, it was 1.6 times.

ref.cite: Singareddy C, Shrestha S, Zheng A, Harlow BL, Barrington-Trimis JL, Harlow AF (2025). Prospective association of symptoms of depression and anxiety with pornography viewing frequency among young adults. Archives of Sexual Behavior 54:749-759.
ref.quote: Participants with comorbid depression and anxiety (vs. no depression or anxiety symptoms) had 2.72 (95% CI: 1.66-4.46) times the odds of frequent pornography viewing (one to several times/day)

stats.line: Among Polish students who watch porn, 46% say they moved on to new genres over time, and 32% to more extreme material.
stats.mirror: You now watch kinds of porn you never searched for at first.

basis.design: online cross-sectional survey; students chose to take part
basis.who: university students aged 18 to 26 who currently watch porn; about 6 in 10 were women
basis.n: 4,260 students who currently watch (1,740 of them men)
basis.measured: Self-reported changes in what they watched since they first saw porn.

stats.caveat: Self-selected students, mostly women, self-report. Shows people's own sense of drift; it does not prove porn causes escalation.

ref.cite: Dwulit AD, Rzymski P (2019). Prevalence, patterns and self-perceived effects of pornography consumption in Polish university students: a cross-sectional study. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health 16:1861.
ref.quote: switching to a novel genre of explicit material (46.0%), use of materials that do not match sexual orientation (60.9%) and need to use more extreme (violent) material (32.0%)

stats.line: Irish men of 20 who watch porn rate their life about 0.4 points lower out of 10, even allowing for how they felt at 17, their internet habits and whether they have a partner.
stats.mirror: You feel flat about life and wonder if porn plays a part.

basis.design: national cohort study (Growing Up in Ireland, Cohort '98), report by the ESRI
basis.who: young men aged 20 (64% of them ticked porn as an internet use)
basis.n: 1,566 men in the fully adjusted model (of 4,585 young adults in the study)
basis.measured: Ticking 'pornography' as one of their internet uses, and life satisfaction on a 0 to 10 scale. −0.372 is the gap after allowing for life satisfaction at 17, having a partner, sexual orientation, internet habits and family background.

stats.caveat: Measured at the same time, so the cause is unclear. Porn use was one yes/no tick. Allowing only for how they felt at 17, the gap was about 0.6.

ref.cite: Nolan A, Smyth E (2024). Use of pornography by young adults in Ireland. ESRI Research Series 177. Dublin: Economic and Social Research Institute.
ref.quote: Males Females Model 1 Model 2 Model 3 Model 1 Model 2 Model 3 Pornography use at 20 −0.649*** −0.635*** −0.372***

stats.line: Married Americans who started watching porn between surveys saw their chance of divorce by the next survey roughly double.
stats.mirror: You're married, started watching porn, and think it's harmless.

basis.design: national panel survey, 3 waves (General Social Survey)
basis.who: married US adults, men and women
basis.n: 2,120 married adults (the study summary doesn't say how many of them started watching porn)
basis.measured: Whether people began using porn between survey waves, and whether they were divorced at the next wave (odds ratio 2.19).

stats.caveat: A link, not proof that porn causes divorce; marriage trouble may come first. Stopping porn went with lower divorce only for women.

ref.cite: Perry SL, Schleifer C (2018). Till porn do us part? A longitudinal examination of pornography use and divorce. Journal of Sex Research 55:284-296.
ref.quote: We found that the probability of divorce roughly doubled for married Americans who began pornography use between survey waves (N = 2,120; odds ratio = 2.19)

stats.line: Even when asked to stop for only 7 days, nearly half of regular users watched porn at least once.
stats.mirror: You slipped in the first week and feel like a failure.

basis.design: randomised controlled trial
basis.who: psychology undergraduates who watched porn 3 or more times a week; 64% women, average age 21
basis.n: 86 asked to stop for 7 days (of 176 in the trial)
basis.measured: Each night for 7 days: craving, good and bad mood, withdrawal symptoms, and any porn use.

stats.caveat: Mostly women students, most with no wish to quit, and slipping cost them nothing. A real, chosen quit attempt may go differently.

ref.cite: Fernandez DP, Kuss DJ, Justice LV, Fernandez EF, Griffiths MD (2023). Effects of a 7-day pornography abstinence period on withdrawal-related symptoms in regular pornography users: a randomized controlled study. Archives of Sexual Behavior 52:1819-1840.
ref.quote: nearly half (45.4%) of participants in the abstinence group reported using pornography at least once during the experimental period

stats.line: About half of Polish students who still watch porn have tried at least once to give it up.
stats.mirror: You've tried to quit before and you're still watching.

basis.design: online cross-sectional survey; students chose to take part
basis.who: university students aged 18 to 26 who currently watch porn; about 6 in 10 were women
basis.n: 4,260 students who still watch (1,740 of them men)
basis.measured: Ever making at least one attempt to stop using porn.

stats.caveat: These are people still watching, so their attempts did not stick. It cannot say how many attempts quitting usually takes.

ref.cite: Dwulit AD, Rzymski P (2019). Prevalence, patterns and self-perceived effects of pornography consumption in Polish university students: a cross-sectional study. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health 16:1861.
ref.quote: 51.0% admitted to making at least one attempt to give up using it with no difference in the frequency of these attempts between males and females

stats.line: Three months after ACT therapy ended, 35% of men had stopped completely and 74% still watched at least 70% less.
stats.mirror: You fear any progress will fade once the help stops.

basis.design: randomised trial, 3-month follow-up (both groups combined after the waitlist group was treated)
basis.who: adult men with problematic internet porn use; all but one were Latter-day Saints
basis.n: 26 men followed up
basis.measured: Self-reported porn viewing at the 3-month follow-up.

stats.caveat: 26 men from one church, self-report, only 3 months. Nothing was reported on mood, sex life or relationships after stopping.

ref.cite: Crosby JM, Twohig MP (2016). Acceptance and commitment therapy for problematic internet pornography use: a randomized trial. Behavior Therapy 47:355-366.
ref.quote: At the 3-month follow-up assessment, 35% of participants showed complete cessation, with 74% of participants showing at least 70% reduction in viewing.

stats.line: Of Polish students who had ever watched porn, 823 of 5,083 (about 1 in 6) said they had successfully stopped; for men alone, 339 of 2,079.
stats.mirror: You doubt anyone really quits porn for good.

basis.design: online cross-sectional survey; students chose to take part
basis.who: university students aged 18 to 26 who had ever seen porn; about 6 in 10 were women
basis.n: 5,083 students who had ever watched (2,079 men); 823 had stopped (339 men)
basis.measured: Saying they had successfully stopped using porn.

stats.caveat: One-time survey; 'stopped' has no time frame, so some may have stopped recently. Says nothing about what improved afterwards.

ref.cite: Dwulit AD, Rzymski P (2019). Prevalence, patterns and self-perceived effects of pornography consumption in Polish university students: a cross-sectional study. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health 16:1861.
ref.quote: while the rest ( n = 823; 484 female and 339 male) reported to successfully cease its use

stats.line: On a quit-porn forum, half of the men who started out with erection trouble wrote that their erections got at least somewhat better after a while without porn.
stats.mirror: You hope quitting porn will fix your erections.

basis.design: study of online quitting journals, with no comparison group
basis.who: men aged 18 to 63 keeping a journal of a quit-porn attempt on the Reboot Nation forum
basis.n: 42 men who wrote about erection trouble at the start (of 104 journals)
basis.measured: What the men wrote about their erections during attempts lasting 7 days to 12 months.

stats.caveat: Their own words, not a doctor's check, and nobody was compared with men who kept watching. Some trouble may have had other causes; large surveys have not found a clear link between porn and erection problems.

ref.cite: Fernandez DP, Kuss DJ, Griffiths MD (2021). The pornography “rebooting” experience: a qualitative analysis of abstinence journals on an online pornography abstinence forum. Archives of Sexual Behavior 50:711-728.
ref.quote: Of the 42 members who reported erectile difficulties at the outset of the abstinence attempt, half (n = 21) reported at least some improvements in erectile function

stats.line: Over 3 years, young adults' scores for out-of-control sex fell on average. At most 31% of a score was fixed; the rest moved with what was going on in life.
stats.mirror: You think you'll be stuck like this for the rest of your life.

basis.design: study that followed a random city sample through 4 rounds over 3 years
basis.who: young adults, average age 27 at the start, who had sex in every round; 60% men
basis.n: 782 young adults
basis.measured: An 8-question test of out-of-control sexual behaviour (porn included) at each round, split into a lasting part and a passing part.

stats.caveat: Most of these people had no serious problem, and the test covers sex in general, not porn alone. It shows that scores move, not who quit or how. A high score did tend to carry over into the next round.

ref.cite: Horváth Z, Bőthe B, Potenza MN, Stein DJ, Demirgül SA, Paksi B, Czakó A, Demetrovics Z (2026). Compulsive sexual behavior may be more state-like than trait-like: findings from a three-year longitudinal representative survey. Journal of Behavioral Addictions 15:622-635.
ref.quote: High proportions of CSB score variance were attributable to state-like/occasion-specific factors (69–93%), while lower proportions of CSB scores were attributable to the trait-like/stable factor (7–31%).

stats.line: Of men who wanted help for their porn use, 4 in 10 had already tried to quit four or more times, and nearly half had tried to cut back four or more times.
stats.mirror: You've tried to quit four times and think a fifth is pointless.

basis.design: online survey
basis.who: men who watch porn, found mostly through Craigslist ads; average age 34
basis.n: 186 men who wanted help for their porn use (of 1,298 surveyed)
basis.where: USA, Canada and other English-speaking countries
basis.measured: Past tries to quit porn completely and to cut back: none, 1 to 3, or 4 or more. Among men who did not want help, 6% had tried to quit four or more times.

stats.caveat: One survey at one moment, so it cannot say whether these men got free later or how many tries quitting usually takes. Volunteers who answered an ad.

ref.cite: Kraus SW, Martino S, Potenza MN (2016). Clinical characteristics of men interested in seeking treatment for use of pornography. Journal of Behavioral Addictions 5:169-178.
ref.quote: treatment-interested men used more pornography (both frequency and duration), had more cut-back attempts with pornography, had more quit attempts with pornography

stats.line: Of people who screened at risk on the strictest problem-porn test, only about 1 in 10 had ever sought help; 1 in 4 said they would have felt too embarrassed.
stats.mirror: You've thought about getting help but felt too embarrassed to ask.

basis.design: international online survey (International Sex Survey)
basis.who: adults of all genders in 42 countries; 3.2% scored at risk on the full Problematic Pornography Consumption Scale
basis.n: about 2,370 people at risk (of 82,243 surveyed)
basis.measured: Ever seeking treatment for porn use (10.2% yes), and the reason for not seeking it ('would have felt uncomfortable or embarrassed': 24.6%). On two looser tests, 4 to 6% had sought treatment.

stats.caveat: Online volunteers, not random national samples. 'At risk' is a screening score, not a diagnosis. Cost and not knowing where to go also held people back.

ref.cite: Bőthe B, Nagy L, Koós M, Demetrovics Z, Potenza MN, International Sex Survey Consortium, Kraus SW (2024). Problematic pornography use across countries, genders, and sexual orientations: insights from the International Sex Survey and comparison of different assessment tools. Addiction 119:928-950.
ref.quote: A total of 4.3–10.2% of the PPU+ group had ever sought treatment for PPU, with an additional 21.0–37.1% wanting to, but not doing so for various reasons (e.g. unaffordability).

stats.line: Of 104 men keeping an online journal while quitting porn, 55 slipped at least once. Half of the attempts they wrote about lasted less than 37 days.
stats.mirror: You broke your streak and think the whole attempt was wasted.

basis.design: study of online quitting journals, with no comparison group
basis.who: men aged 18 to 63 on the Reboot Nation forum; 77% called themselves addicted to porn
basis.n: 104 men (55 slipped at least once)
basis.measured: Slips the men wrote about, and how long each attempt lasted (7 days to 12 months). At least 86.5% were also trying to stop masturbating.

stats.caveat: Many men just stopped writing, so nobody knows how their attempts ended. Men who journal in public may differ from men who quit quietly.

ref.cite: Fernandez DP, Kuss DJ, Griffiths MD (2021). The pornography “rebooting” experience: a qualitative analysis of abstinence journals on an online pornography abstinence forum. Archives of Sexual Behavior 50:711-728.
ref.quote: More than half of the sample (n = 55) reported at least one lapse during their abstinence attempt.

stats.line: Of the common kinds of quit-porn app, blockers had the most installs: at least 17.9 million. None of the 170 apps checked pointed to proof that it works.
stats.mirror: You've installed a blocker and wonder whether it's enough on its own.

basis.design: review of app-store listings
basis.who: apps that said they help people cut down or stop porn
basis.n: 170 apps (46 offered blocking or monitoring)
basis.where: Google Play and the Apple App Store
basis.measured: The features in each app's store description, and the lowest install count the store showed, added up per feature.

stats.caveat: Installs count Android downloads only, not people, and say nothing about who quit. Men on a quit-porn forum found blockers easy to get around, but useful as one extra hurdle in a weak moment.

ref.cite: Henry N, Donkin L, Williams M, Pedersen M (2022). mHealth technologies for managing problematic pornography use: content analysis. JMIR Formative Research 6:e39869.
ref.quote: content blocking and monitoring, was only included as a feature on 27.1% (46/170) of the apps but had the highest minimum number of installations at 17,883,000

stats.line: People who got talk therapy for porn problems, mostly CBT or ACT, cut their problem use clearly more than people who didn't. Only 3 small trials tested that head to head.
stats.mirror: You wonder if therapy really works for porn or just costs money.

basis.design: meta-analysis of 20 studies, 5 of them randomised trials
basis.who: people with problem porn use; 84% men, average age 31
basis.n: 98 people in the 3 trials behind this comparison (2,021 in all 20 studies)
basis.measured: Problem porn use after therapy, compared with control groups (waiting list or other help). The gap was large by research standards; for craving it was small.

stats.caveat: Every study was judged at high or some risk of bias, and most had no control group at all. A bigger, careful trial could find a smaller effect.

ref.cite: López-Pinar C, Esparza-Reig J, Bőthe B (2025). Psychotherapy for problematic pornography use: a comprehensive meta-analysis. Journal of Behavioral Addictions 14:630-643.
ref.quote: Participants receiving psychotherapy improved significantly more than controls on PPU, frequency/duration of pornography use, and sexual compulsivity, with large effect sizes, that were small for craving.

stats.line: Men who had seen a professional about their porn use rated the help 2.7 on a 5-point scale; the researchers call that only marginally helpful. About half still wanted help.
stats.mirror: You saw a therapist about porn and it didn't fix it.

basis.design: online survey
basis.who: men who watch porn, found mostly through Craigslist ads; average age 34
basis.n: 83 men who had ever seen a professional about porn (of 1,298 surveyed)
basis.where: USA, Canada and other English-speaking countries
basis.measured: How helpful their counsellor, therapist, psychologist or psychiatrist was, from 'not at all' to 'extremely' helpful. 40 of the 83 still wanted help.

stats.caveat: Men still struggling are more likely to answer a survey like this, so it may undersell therapy. It says nothing about what kind of help they got or for how long.

ref.cite: Kraus SW, Martino S, Potenza MN (2016). Clinical characteristics of men interested in seeking treatment for use of pornography. Journal of Behavioral Addictions 5:169-178.
ref.quote: Fewer men (6.4%, n = 83) reported having previously sought treatment for use of pornography, and on average, those who had received treatment rated it as only marginally helpful

stats.line: In a small trial, 12 sessions of ACT therapy cut porn viewing by 93%, against 21% for men on a waiting list.
stats.mirror: You've tried willpower alone and want a method that works.

basis.design: randomised trial (ACT therapy vs waiting list)
basis.who: adult men with problematic internet porn use; all but one were Latter-day Saints
basis.n: 28 men, split between therapy and a waiting list
basis.measured: Self-reported porn viewing before and after 12 one-to-one sessions.

stats.caveat: Only 28 men, almost all from one church, self-reported viewing, no comparison therapy. Promising, not proven.

ref.cite: Crosby JM, Twohig MP (2016). Acceptance and commitment therapy for problematic internet pornography use: a randomized trial. Behavior Therapy 47:355-366.
ref.quote: significant between-condition reductions in pornography viewing compared to the waitlist condition (93% reduction ACT vs. 21% waitlist)

rejected.claim: Porn causes erectile dysfunction in young men.
rejected.why: Grubbs & Gola 2019 (3 US samples of men, J Sex Med, PMID 30621919, fetched): simple use was not consistently linked to erection problems, and over a year no porn variable predicted change. Feeling your use is a problem was linked cross-sectionally only.

rejected.claim: Quitting porn and masturbation lowers fatigue and boosts energy and self-control (NoFap-style benefit).
rejected.why: Only source found: Straub & Schmidt 2022, 21 single men, Journal of Addiction Science (not a PubMed-indexed journal); far too small and weak to put a number on the page.

rejected.claim: Quitting porn lifts mood (a number for the 'after' group).
rejected.why: No study measured this. A US study of 4,363 adults over a year (Engelhardt 2025, PMID 40483829, fetched) found problem porn use and distress linked as a stable trait; the over-time (cross-lagged) effects were small and negative.

rejected.claim: Hands-off online self-help cut problem porn use strongly (d = 1.32).
rejected.why: Bőthe 2021 trial (PMID 34727088, fetched): 89.4% of the self-help group dropped out; only 11% gave follow-up data. Too few to trust.

rejected.claim: Imaginal retraining reduces problem porn use.
rejected.why: Baumeister 2024 trial (PMID 38669086, fetched): the effect showed only among those who did the training; the intention-to-treat analysis did not confirm it.

rejected.claim: About 20% of US men watched porn daily in 2019 (Porndemic study).
rejected.why: Grubbs 2022 (PMID 34282505, fetched): the table conflicts with the text (62% 'never' vs 43.4% not in past year) and later waves show about 6 to 7%; used the 2019 national figure of 8% instead.

rejected.claim: 72% of people who try to quit porn get withdrawal effects (irritability 26%, attention problems 26%).
rejected.why: Dwulit 2019 (fetched): remembered, self-selected student survey, mostly women; 'erotic dreams' counted as an effect. A randomised trial found no withdrawal over 7 days. Not used as a number.

rejected.claim: About 1 in 8 US men agree they have put off things they needed to do so they could watch porn.
rejected.why: A sum of three table cells, not a number the study states. Left out to keep every number as printed in its source.

rejected.claim: Irish men of 20 who watch porn rate their life 0.6 points lower out of 10.
rejected.why: ESRI 2024 (fetched): −0.635 allows only for life satisfaction at 17. The fully adjusted model (internet use, partner, orientation) gives −0.372, so the page shows 0.4.

rejected.claim: Only 4 to 10% of people at risk of problem porn use had ever sought treatment.
rejected.why: Bőthe 2024 (full text fetched): the range spans three screening tests. The page uses the strictest test (10.2% of about 2,370 at-risk people), so the number has one clear group behind it.

rejected.claim: Group CBT cut hypersexual symptoms in 137 Swedish men (Hallberg 2019, J Sex Med).
rejected.why: PMID 30956109 abstract fetched: randomised and all men, but it gives no size for the effect and the full text is paywalled; follow-up response was low. No number to show.

rejected.claim: Internet CBT for hypersexual disorder in 36 men brought large drops in symptoms (Hallberg 2020).
rejected.why: PMID 32900671 abstract fetched: no control group and no figure in the summary.

rejected.claim: 64% of men in a Reddit survey had tried to stop masturbating (Zimmer & Imhoff 2020, NoFap-style).
rejected.why: PMC7145784 fetched: about masturbation, not porn; the wish to stop tracked seeing masturbation as unhealthy, not how much sex people had. Off this page's angle.

rejected.claim: Feeling addicted to porn a year later tracks moral disapproval more than hours watched (Grubbs 2018, Addiction).
rejected.why: PMID 28833800 abstract fetched: about who feels hooked, not about how people quit; the page no longer screens.

rejected.claim: Aiming to cut down works as well as (or worse than) quitting porn completely.
rejected.why: Searched PubMed: no study compares the two goals for porn. Forum men saw moderation as unworkable (Fernandez 2021), but that is opinion, not a number.

rejected.claim: Medication (naltrexone, SSRIs) helps men quit porn.
rejected.why: Only case reports so far; the 410-man escitalopram and naltrexone trial (PMID 42919590, fetched) is a protocol with no results yet.

rejected.claim: Treatment for problem porn use: 28 studies, 500 people, all evidence rated low or very low (Roza 2024).
rejected.why: PMID 37880509 abstract fetched: mostly case reports and no pooled size. The 2025 meta-analysis covers the same trials with sizes; its caveat carries the bias warning.

rejected.claim: Only 35% of 186 clinicians said porn treatment was somewhat successful, 9.3% very (cited in López-Pinar 2025).
rejected.why: Second-hand: the original clinician survey was not fetched, so the figure is not used.
